claim: The C-terminal tail of Twinfilin harbors a CP-interacting (CPI) motif.
source: Here, we discover that the C-terminal tail of Twinfilin harbors a CP-interacting (CPI) motif, identifying it as a novel CPI-motif protein.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 2A) and binding assays (Figure 2B-D) showing competition between Twinfilin and CARMIL CPI motif for CP binding.

claim: Twinfilin and CARMIL have overlapping binding sites on CP.
source: Twinfilin and the CPI-motif protein CARMIL have overlapping binding sites on CP.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition assays (Figure 2D) and HDX-MS data (Figure 5) showing similar regions of CP are protected from deuterium exchange by both Twinfilin and CARMIL.

claim: Twinfilin binds competitively with CARMIL to CP.
source: Further, Twinfilin binds competitively with CARMIL to CP, protecting CP from barbed-end displacement by CARMIL.
evidence: Demonstrated by fluorescence anisotropy showing CARMIL CBR competes with mTwf1 tail for CP binding (Figure 2D) and TIRF microscopy showing mTwf1 attenuates CARMIL-mediated CP displacement (Figure 3B-C).

claim: Twinfilin protects CP from barbed-end displacement by CARMIL.
source: Further, Twinfilin binds competitively with CARMIL to CP, protecting CP from barbed-end displacement by CARMIL.
evidence: Shown by TIRF microscopy experiments where increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuate CARMIL-induced uncapping of barbed ends (Figure 3A-C).

claim: Twinfilin accelerates dissociation of the CP inhibitor V-1.
source: Twinfilin also accelerates dissociation of the CP inhibitor V-1, restoring CP to an active capping state.
evidence: Demonstrated by stopped-flow fluorescence assays showing mTwf1 increases the rate of V-1 dissociation from CP in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4D-E).

claim: Knockdowns of Twinfilin and CP each cause similar defects in cell morphology.
source: Knockdowns of Twinfilin and CP each cause similar defects in cell morphology, and elevated Twinfilin expression rescues defects caused by CARMIL hyperactivity.
evidence: Shown by RNAi silencing experiments in B16F10 cells where both mTwf1 and CP knockdown led to increased density of peripheral protrusions or microspikes (Figure 6F-G).

claim: Elevated Twinfilin expression rescues defects caused by CARMIL hyperactivity.
source: Knockdowns of Twinfilin and CP each cause similar defects in cell morphology, and elevated Twinfilin expression rescues defects caused by CARMIL hyperactivity.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued morphological defects caused by CARMIL1 overexpression in B16F10 cells (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Twinfilin is the first 'pro-capping' ligand of CP.
source: Together, these observations define Twinfilin as the first 'pro-capping' ligand of CP and lead us to propose important revisions to our understanding of the CP regulatory cycle.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the collective data showing Twinfilin protects CP from inhibitors (V-1 and CARMIL) rather than inhibiting CP itself.

claim: Twinfilin is one of five proteins in the Actin Depolymerization Factor-Homology (ADF-H) domain family.
source: Twinfilin is one of five proteins in the Actin Depolymerization Factor-Homology (ADF-H) domain family, of which ADF/Cofilin is the founding member (Poukkula et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poukkula et al., 2011.

claim: Twinfilin is unique among ADF-H domain family members in containing two ADF-H domains.
source: Twinfilin is unique among the members of this family in containing two ADF-H domains, which are joined by a small linker region and followed by a short C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is a structural description supported by established knowledge of Twinfilin domain organization (Figure 1A).

claim: Initial biochemical studies categorized Twinfilin as an actin monomer sequestering factor.
source: Initial biochemical studies categorized Twinfilin as an actin monomer sequestering factor because of its high affinity for ADP-bound G-actin and ability to inhibit subunit addition to either end of the filament (Goode et al., 1998; Vartiainen et al., 2000; Wahlström et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Goode et al., 1998; Vartiainen et al., 2000; Wahlström et al., 2001).

claim: Mouse Twinfilin was shown to interact directly with the barbed ends of actin filaments.
source: However, mouse Twinfilin was later shown to interact directly with the barbed ends of actin filaments (Helfer et al., 2006; Paavilainen et al., 2007), and more recently yeast Twinfilin was shown to accelerate depolymerization at actin filament ends (Johnston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Helfer et al., 2006 and Paavilainen et al., 2007.

claim: Yeast Twinfilin was shown to accelerate depolymerization at actin filament ends.
source: However, mouse Twinfilin was later shown to interact directly with the barbed ends of actin filaments (Helfer et al., 2006; Paavilainen et al., 2007), and more recently yeast Twinfilin was shown to accelerate depolymerization at actin filament ends (Johnston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnston et al., 2015.

claim: Yeast Twinfilin enhanced barbed end depolymerization by 3-fold through a processive filament end-attachment mechanism.
source: Alone, yeast Twinfilin enhanced barbed end depolymerization by 3-fold through a processive filament end-attachment mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on previous work cited in the manuscript (Johnston et al., 2015).

claim: In conjunction with Srv2/CAP, yeast Twinfilin increased the rate of pointed-end depolymerization by over 15-fold.
source: Further, in conjunction with Srv2/CAP (cyclase-associated protein), yeast Twinfilin increased the rate of pointed-end depolymerization by over 15-fold (Johnston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnston et al., 2015.

claim: Mouse Twinfilin isoforms accelerate barbed end depolymerization, similar to yeast Twinfilin.
source: More recently, it was shown that mouse Twinfilin isoforms accelerate barbed end depolymerization, similar to yeast Twinfilin, but do not induce robust pointed end depolymerization in conjunction with Srv2/CAP (Hilton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilton et al., 2018.

claim: Mouse Twinfilin isoforms do not induce robust pointed end depolymerization in conjunction with Srv2/CAP.
source: More recently, it was shown that mouse Twinfilin isoforms accelerate barbed end depolymerization, similar to yeast Twinfilin, but do not induce robust pointed end depolymerization in conjunction with Srv2/CAP (Hilton et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilton et al., 2018.

claim: Both yeast and mammalian Twinfilins bind to CP.
source: The conserved barbed-end effects of Twinfilin are particularly interesting given that both yeast and mammalian Twinfilins bind to CP (Falck et al., 2004; Palmgren et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Falck et al., 2004 and Palmgren et al., 2001.

claim: Twinfilin localizes to the tips of stereocilia and filopodia.
source: Further, a barbed-end regulatory role for Twinfilin is suggested by its localization to the tips of stereocilia and filopodia, and to the barbed ends of Drosophila actin bristles (Peng et al., 2009; Rzadzinska et al., 2009; Wahlström et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2009; Rzadzinska et al., 2009; Wahlström et al., 2001.

claim: Twinfilin localizes to the barbed ends of Drosophila actin bristles.
source: Further, a barbed-end regulatory role for Twinfilin is suggested by its localization to the tips of stereocilia and filopodia, and to the barbed ends of Drosophila actin bristles (Peng et al., 2009; Rzadzinska et al., 2009; Wahlström et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2009; Rzadzinska et al., 2009; Wahlström et al., 2001.

claim: Twinfilin localizes to endocytic actin patches in yeast.
source: In addition, Twinfilin localizes to endocytic actin patches in yeast, and to lamellipodia and cell-cell junctions in animal cells (Goode et al., 1998; Vartiainen et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goode et al., 1998 and Vartiainen et al., 2000.

claim: Twinfilin localizes to lamellipodia and cell-cell junctions in animal cells.
source: In addition, Twinfilin localizes to endocytic actin patches in yeast, and to lamellipodia and cell-cell junctions in animal cells (Goode et al., 1998; Vartiainen et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goode et al., 1998 and Vartiainen et al., 2000.

claim: Twinfilin's localization to cortical actin patches in yeast is dependent on its interaction with CP.
source: Twinfilin's localization to cortical actin patches in yeast is dependent on its interaction with CP (Palmgren et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Palmgren et al., 2001.

claim: In both yeast and mammals, the Twinfilin-CP interaction is mediated by conserved sequences in the C-terminal tail region of Twinfilin.
source: In both yeast and mammals, this interaction is mediated by conserved sequences in the C-terminal tail region of Twinfilin (Falck et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Falck et al., 2004.

claim: The Twinfilin-CP interaction has a Kd of ~10 nM for the yeast homologs.
source: Despite the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd ~10 nM for the yeast homologs [Poukkula et al., 2011]), studies have revealed no significant effects of Twinfilin on the barbed end capping activity of CP in vitro, and reciprocally, no obvious effect of CP on Twinfilin interactions with ADP-actin monomers (Falck et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Poukkula et al., 2011.

claim: Studies have revealed no significant effects of Twinfilin on the barbed end capping activity of CP in vitro.
source: Despite the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd ~10 nM for the yeast homologs [Poukkula et al., 2011]), studies have revealed no significant effects of Twinfilin on the barbed end capping activity of CP in vitro, and reciprocally, no obvious effect of CP on Twinfilin interactions with ADP-actin monomers (Falck et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Falck et al., 2004.

claim: CP has no obvious effect on Twinfilin interactions with ADP-actin monomers.
source: Despite the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd ~10 nM for the yeast homologs [Poukkula et al., 2011]), studies have revealed no significant effects of Twinfilin on the barbed end capping activity of CP in vitro, and reciprocally, no obvious effect of CP on Twinfilin interactions with ADP-actin monomers (Falck et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Falck et al., 2004.

claim: CP is an obligate heterodimer, consisting of alpha and beta subunits.
source: CP is an obligate heterodimer, consisting of alpha and beta subunits, and binds stably to the barbed ends of actin filaments to block subunit addition and loss.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CP structure.

claim: CP binds stably to the barbed ends of actin filaments to block subunit addition and loss.
source: CP is an obligate heterodimer, consisting of alpha and beta subunits, and binds stably to the barbed ends of actin filaments to block subunit addition and loss.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CP function.

claim: CP is ubiquitous and highly conserved across eukaryotes.
source: CP is ubiquitous and highly conserved across eukaryotes, and has universal roles in controlling the assembly of actin networks that drive cell morphogenesis and cell motility (Cooper and Sept, 2008; Hart and Cooper, 1999; Mejillano et al., 2004; Schafer et al., 1994; Schafer et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Cooper and Sept, 2008; Hart and Cooper, 1999; Mejillano et al., 2004; Schafer et al., 1994; Schafer et al., 1995).

claim: CP has universal roles in controlling the assembly of actin networks that drive cell morphogenesis and cell motility.
source: CP is ubiquitous and highly conserved across eukaryotes, and has universal roles in controlling the assembly of actin networks that drive cell morphogenesis and cell motility (Cooper and Sept, 2008; Hart and Cooper, 1999; Mejillano et al., 2004; Schafer et al., 1994; Schafer et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Cooper and Sept, 2008; Hart and Cooper, 1999; Mejillano et al., 2004; Schafer et al., 1994; Schafer et al., 1995).

claim: In vitro, CP binds to the barbed ends of actin filaments with sub-nanomolar affinity.
source: In vitro, CP binds to the barbed ends of actin filaments with sub-nanomolar affinity, and dissociates from barbed ends very slowly (half-life of ~30 min) (Schafer et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schafer et al., 1996.

claim: CP dissociates from barbed ends very slowly with a half-life of ~30 min.
source: In vitro, CP binds to the barbed ends of actin filaments with sub-nanomolar affinity, and dissociates from barbed ends very slowly (half-life of ~30 min) (Schafer et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schafer et al., 1996.

claim: CP is present at relatively high abundance in the cytosol (1–3 µM).
source: Given the relatively high abundance of CP in the cytosol (1–3 µM) and the strength of its interactions with barbed ends (Cooper and Sept, 2008), it is not surprising that cells have evolved a number of regulatory mechanisms to spatiotemporally restrict CP activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cooper and Sept, 2008.

claim: Cellular protein inhibitors of CP broadly fall into two classes: steric inhibitors and allosteric inhibitors.
source: Cellular protein inhibitors of CP broadly fall into two classes: steric inhibitors and allosteric inhibitors.
evidence: This is a classification based on established knowledge of CP regulation.

claim: Steric inhibitors bind to CP in a manner that physically obstructs its association with barbed ends.
source: Steric inhibitors, which include V-1/myotrophin, bind to CP in a manner that physically obstructs its association with barbed ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2007; Schafer et al., 1996.

claim: V-1 is a highly abundant 13 kDa protein that binds CP with a Kd ~40 nM.
source: V-1 is a highly abundant 13 kDa protein that binds CP with a Kd ~40 nM and sterically blocks its ability to bind barbed ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Taoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2006 and Taoka et al., 2003.

claim: V-1 sterically blocks CP's ability to bind barbed ends.
source: V-1 is a highly abundant 13 kDa protein that binds CP with a Kd ~40 nM and sterically blocks its ability to bind barbed ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Taoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2006 and Taoka et al., 2003.

claim: V-1 does not catalyze dissociation of CP from barbed ends.
source: Notably, however, V-1 does not catalyze dissociation of CP from barbed ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bhattacharya et al., 2006.

claim: Allosteric inhibitors induce conformational changes in CP that catalyze its dissociation from barbed ends.
source: In contrast, allosteric inhibitors induce conformational changes in CP that catalyze its dissociation from barbed ends ('uncapping' or 'displacing' CP), and also decrease but do not abolish its ability to bind barbed ends.
evidence: This is established knowledge about allosteric inhibitors of CP.

claim: The major class of allosteric inhibitors is the capping protein interaction (CPI) motif family of proteins.
source: The major class of allosteric inhibitors is the capping protein interaction (CPI) motif family of proteins (Edwards et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2014.

claim: CARMIL is the founding and best characterized member of the CPI family.
source: The founding and best characterized member of the CPI family is CARMIL (Capping Protein, ARP2/3 and Myosin I linker), which is conserved across metazoans (Stark et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stark et al., 2017.

claim: CARMIL is conserved across metazoans.
source: The founding and best characterized member of the CPI family is CARMIL (Capping Protein, ARP2/3 and Myosin I linker), which is conserved across metazoans (Stark et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stark et al., 2017.

claim: CARMIL catalyzes CP dissociation from barbed ends, reducing CP's affinity for barbed ends by ~100 fold.
source: CARMIL catalyzes CP dissociation from barbed ends, reducing CP's affinity for barbed ends by ~100 fold, transforming it into a transient capper (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2017; Uruno et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2014; Stark et al., 2017; Uruno et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2005.

claim: CARMIL localizes to the leading-edge plasma membrane.
source: CARMIL localizes to the leading-edge plasma membrane, where it promotes cell migration through direct interactions with CP (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2005.

claim: CARMIL promotes cell migration through direct interactions with CP.
source: CARMIL localizes to the leading-edge plasma membrane, where it promotes cell migration through direct interactions with CP (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2009; Stark et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2005.

claim: Other proteins with CPI motifs include CD2AP, CKIP-1, CapZIP, CIN85, and WASHCAP (FAM21).
source: Other proteins with CPI motifs include CD2AP, CKIP-1, CapZIP, CIN85, and WASHCAP (FAM21); their roles in regulating CP are less well understood.
evidence: This is a statement of known CPI-motif proteins.

claim: CPI-motif proteins share a common mode of interaction with CP, but are otherwise unrelated to each other.
source: CPI-motif proteins share a common mode of interaction with CP, but are otherwise unrelated to each other (Edwards et al., 2014; Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2014 and Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010.

claim: Binding partners of CP that antagonize its inhibitors, and thus function as 'pro-capping' factors, have not been reported prior to this study.
source: To date, binding partners of CP that antagonize its inhibitors, and thus function as 'pro-capping' factors, have not been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The mTwf1 tail peptide displayed high affinity, concentration-dependent binding to CPα1β2.
source: The mTwf1 tail peptide displayed high affinity, concentration-dependent binding to CPα1β2, a major non-muscle isoform of CP in mammalian cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Full-length mTwf1 protein competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
source: Moreover, full-length mTwf1 protein (unlabeled) competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding, whereas full-length mTwf1-11 (unlabeled) did not (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Full-length mTwf1-11 did not compete with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
source: Moreover, full-length mTwf1 protein (unlabeled) competed with the labeled mTwf1 tail for CP binding, whereas full-length mTwf1-11 (unlabeled) did not (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mTwf1-11 mutant effectively uncouples mTwf1 binding to CP.
source: Thus, the mTwf1-11 mutant effectively uncouples mTwf1 binding to CP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data showing mTwf1-11 does not compete for CP binding (Figure 1C).

claim: 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions.
source: In agreement with previous observations using yeast and mouse Twinfilin (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015), 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions (Figure 1D), and the addition of CP blocked this effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The addition of CP blocked the mTwf1-mediated acceleration of barbed end depolymerization.
source: In agreement with previous observations using yeast and mouse Twinfilin (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015), 1 µM mTwf1 accelerated barbed end depolymerization by 2–3 fold compared to control reactions (Figure 1D), and the addition of CP blocked this effect (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar depolymerization rate to wild-type mTwf1.
source: Further, mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar rate (Figure 1D), indicating that this mutant has wild type depolymerization activity, and thus separates Twinfilin's ability to bind CP from its ability to promote barbed-end depolymerization.
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The mTwf1-11 mutant has wild type depolymerization activity.
source: Further, mTwf1-11 exhibited a similar rate (Figure 1D), indicating that this mutant has wild type depolymerization activity, and thus separates Twinfilin's ability to bind CP from its ability to promote barbed-end depolymerization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar depolymerization rates observed for mTwf1 and mTwf1-11 (Figure 1D).

claim: The addition of CP was able to block barbed-end depolymerization by mTwf1-11.
source: Interestingly, the addition of CP was still able to block barbed-end depolymerization by mTwf1-11 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CP sterically blocks mTwf1 access to barbed ends, independent of its direct interaction with mTwf1.
source: These observations suggest that CP sterically blocks mTwf1 access to barbed ends, independent of its direct interaction with mTwf1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CP blocks both mTwf1 and mTwf1-11 depolymerization activity (Figure 1E).

claim: The mTwf1 tail interacted equally well with wild-type CP and CPαΔ28.
source: Importantly, in binding assays the mTwf1 tail interacted equally well with wild-type CP and CPαΔ28, demonstrating that this mutant binds normally to mTwf1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity.
source: In TIRF assays, equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 1; also summarized in Figure 1G), suggesting that while CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and summarized in Figure 1G.

claim: While CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
source: In TIRF assays, equimolar amounts of CPαΔ28 did not significantly alter mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F; Figure 1—video 1; also summarized in Figure 1G), suggesting that while CP blocks Twinfilin access to barbed ends, Twinfilin-CP direct interaction does not alter Twinfilin depolymerization activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CPαΔ28 (which binds mTwf1 but doesn't cap) doesn't affect mTwf1 depolymerization activity (Figure 1F-G).

claim: The C-terminal tail regions of evolutionarily diverse Twinfilins share sequence homology with the CPI motifs of several CPI family proteins.
source: We were particularly interested in how Twinfilin might impact the regulation of CP by CPI-motif proteins such as CARMIL, since we noticed that the C-terminal tail regions of evolutionarily diverse Twinfilins share sequence homology with the CPI motifs of several CPI family proteins (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The consensus CPI motif is 17-amino acids long.
source: The consensus CPI motif is 17-amino acids long, with some additional contacts contributed from outside this motif, and tolerates significant divergence across the CPI-motif family (Edwards et al., 2014; Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2014 and Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010.

claim: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL.
source: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL and disrupts binding with at least two other CPI-motif proteins, CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21) (Edwards et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2015.

claim: The CP(RY) mutant disrupts binding with CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21).
source: The CP(RY) mutant is insensitive to inhibition and uncapping by CARMIL and disrupts binding with at least two other CPI-motif proteins, CD2AP and WASHCAP (FAM21) (Edwards et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Edwards et al., 2015.

claim: The CP(RY) mutant has approximately 20-fold reduced affinity for mTwf1 tail compared to wild type CP.
source: In fluorescence anisotropy binding assays, we observed that the CP(RY) mutant has approximately 20-fold reduced affinity for mTwf1 tail compared to wild type CP (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mTwf1 and CPI-motif proteins share at least partially overlapping binding sites on CP.
source: These data are consistent with mTwf1 and CPI-motif proteins sharing at least partially overlapping binding sites on CP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced binding of mTwf1 tail to CP(RY) mutant (Figure 2B).

claim: The mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptide showed an ~30 fold reduction in binding affinity for CP compared to wild type peptide.
source: In fluorescence anisotropy binding assays, we compared the abilities of wild-type and mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptides to compete with labeled mTwf1 tail peptide for CP binding. This analysis revealed an ~30 fold reduction in binding affinity for the mutant (K325A) mTwf1 tail peptide compared to wild type peptide (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Unlabeled CBR peptide competed with the fluorescent mTwf1 tail probe for CP binding.
source: We next asked whether the CP-binding region (CBR) of CARMIL1 (residues 964 – 1078) competes with mTwf1 tail for binding to CP. We observed that unlabeled CBR peptide competed with the fluorescent mTwf1 tail probe for CP binding (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CARMIL and mTwf1 directly compete for binding CP.
source: These results indicate that CARMIL and mTwf1 directly compete for binding CP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only the CPI-motif peptide and not the CSI peptide competed with mTwf1 tail for CP binding.
source: As expected based on Twinfilin's sequence similarity to CPI motifs, only the CPI-motif peptide and not the CSI peptide competed with mTwf1 tail for CP binding (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy competition data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Twinfilin is a divergent CPI-motif protein.
source: Together, these results suggest that Twinfilin is a divergent CPI-motif protein and has important implications for CP regulation in cells (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective binding and competition data (Figures 2A-D).

claim: Increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuated CARMIL's uncapping effects.
source: CARMIL1 alone (no mTwf1) strongly induced uncapping, leading to the rapid polymerization of previously-capped filament seeds (Figure 3A). However, increasing concentrations of mTwf1 attenuated CARMIL's uncapping effects (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene actin assembly assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: mTwf1 competes with CARMIL for binding CP, thereby blocking uncapping.
source: These results are consistent with mTwf1 competing with CARMIL for binding CP, and thereby blocking uncapping.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pyrene actin assembly data (Figure 3A).

claim: CARMIL1 CBR led to the rapid displacement of SNAP-649-CP, with complete loss of CP from barbed ends by 100 s.
source: As expected, in the absence of other factors, SNAP-649-CP had a long dwell time, remaining on barbed ends for tens of minutes (Figure 3B and C). However, when CARMIL1 CBR was introduced, this led to the rapid displacement of SNAP-649-CP, with complete loss of CP from barbed ends by 100 s (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C.

claim: The addition of mTwf1 with CARMIL1 CBR attenuated the uncapping effects in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: The addition of mTwf1 with CARMIL1 CBR attenuated the uncapping effects in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C.

claim: The attenuation of CARMIL uncapping by Twinfilin required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP.
source: Further, this attenuation required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP, as mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data showing mTwf1-11 does not protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D-E).

claim: mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping.
source: Further, this attenuation required direct interactions between Twinfilin and CP, as mTwf1-11 failed to protect CP from CARMIL uncapping (Figure 3D and E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Similar protective effects against CARMIL uncapping were observed for mTwf2a.
source: Similar effects were observed for the other major isoform of mouse Twinfilin that is expressed in non-muscle cells, mTwf2a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Nevalainen et al., 2011; Vartiainen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: V-1 does not displace CP from barbed ends; instead, it sequesters CP and blocks it from binding filament ends.
source: Unlike CARMIL, V-1 does not displace CP from barbed ends; instead, it sequesters CP and blocks it from binding filament ends (Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Jung et al., 2016; Taoka et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2006; Jung et al., 2016; Taoka et al., 2003.

claim: V-1 interacts with CP on the opposite face from CARMIL, sterically blocking binding to the filament end.
source: In contrast to the CARMIL binding site on CP, which partially encircles the 'stalk' of the CP heterodimer (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010; Johnson et al., 2018; Zwolak et al., 2010), V-1 interacts with CP on the opposite face, sterically blocking binding to the filament end (Johnson et al., 2018; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2018; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010.

claim: The addition of V-1 to CP-capped filament seeds restored actin assembly to uncapped levels.
source: As expected, filament seeds pre-incubated with CP and then mixed with pyrene-actin monomers displayed minimal growth, whereas the addition of V-1 restored actin assembly to uncapped levels.
evidence: This is based on pyrene-actin seeded elongation assays (Figure 4A).

claim: The further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity.
source: Somewhat to our surprise, the further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity, while mTwf1-11 had no effect (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene-actin seeded elongation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: mTwf1-11 had no effect on V-1's inhibition of CP.
source: Somewhat to our surprise, the further addition of mTwf1 suppressed V-1's effects, restoring capping activity, while mTwf1-11 had no effect (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pyrene-actin seeded elongation assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Even high concentrations of V-1 (1000-fold excess to mTwf1 tail probe) fail to compete with mTwf1 for CP binding.
source: These effects were unexpected given the above-mentioned differences in Twinfilin's predicted and V-1's known binding sites on CP, and our observation that even high concentrations of V-1 (1000-fold excess to mTwf1 tail probe) fail to compete with mTwf1 for CP binding in anisotropy assays (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mTwf1 attenuates V-1 effects on CP via an allosteric mechanism, distinct from a simple steric binding competition.
source: These results suggest that mTwf1 attenuates V-1 effects on CP via an allosteric mechanism, distinct from a simple steric binding competition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that V-1 doesn't compete with mTwf1 for CP binding (Figure 4C) yet mTwf1 affects V-1 function (Figure 4A).

claim: CARMIL forms a transient ternary complex with V-1 and CP, leading to accelerated dissociation of V-1 from CP.
source: In probing the mechanism further, we drew inspiration from a study by Fujiwara and colleagues, showing that CARMIL forms a transient ternary complex with V-1 and CP, leading to accelerated dissociation of V-1 from CP (Fujiwara et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fujiwara et al., 2014.

claim: The rate of V-1 dissociation from CP increased in the presence of increasing concentrations of mTwf1.
source: The rate of V-1 dissociation from CP increased in the presence of increasing concentrations of mTwf1, pointing to the possible formation of a transient ternary complex that destabilizes V-1 interactions with CP (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation from CP.
source: Importantly, mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E), showing that this effect depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
evidence: This claim is supported by stopped-flow fluorescence assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The effect of mTwf1 on V-1 dissociation depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
source: Importantly, mTwf1-11 failed to enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E), showing that this effect depends on direct interactions between mTwf1 tail and CP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mTwf1-11 (which doesn't bind CP) doesn't enhance V-1 dissociation (Figure 4E).

claim: CARMIL and Twinfilin share a common function in catalyzing the dissociation of V-1 from CP using their CPI motifs to bind CP.
source: These results demonstrate that CARMIL and Twinfilin share a common function in catalyzing the dissociation of V-1 from CP using their CPI motifs to bind CP, despite having different effects on the displacement of CP from barbed ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data showing both CARMIL and Twinfilin accelerate V-1 dissociation from CP.

claim: The presence of mTwf1 resulted in protection from H-D exchange at the N-terminal stalk of CP.
source: The results were essentially the same in each case. The presence of mTwf1 resulted in protection from H-D exchange at the N-terminal stalk of CP (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Similar H-D exchange protection effects were observed upon CARMIL binding to CP.
source: Similar effects to H-D exchange were observed upon CARMIL binding to CP (Johnson et al., 2018); also shown here in Figure 5B), which correspond well with the CPI-motif binding site defined by X-ray crystallography and solution NMR studies (Hernandez-Valladares et al., 2010; Takeda et al., 2010; Zwolak et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2018 and HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: mTwf1 binding caused H-D exchange protection of a small region on CP corresponding to the V-1 binding site.
source: For mTwf1, we also observed H-D exchange protection of a small region on CP corresponding to the V-1 binding site (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2), consistent with our results described above for the effects of mTwf1 in promoting V-1 dissociation from CP.
evidence: This claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5A-B and supplementary figures.

claim: mTwf1-induced changes in CP conformation at the actin-binding interface were not as extensive as those induced by CARMIL.
source: However, it is worth noting that mTwf1-induced changes in CP conformation at the actin-binding interface were not as extensive as those induced by CARMIL, which is consistent with CARMIL, but not mTwf1, weakening CP binding to actin at the barbed ends.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of HDX-MS data for mTwf1 and CARMIL binding to CP (Figure 5A-B).

claim: Strong colocalization of Twinfilin and CP was observed throughout B16F10 cells with co-enrichment at the actin-rich leading and trailing edges.
source: We observed strong colocalization of Twinfilin and CP throughout the cell and a co-enrichment at the actin-rich leading and trailing edges (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Twinfilin and CP are present at ~1:2 molar ratio in B16F10 cells.
source: Further, quantitative western blotting showed that Twinfilin and CP are present at ~1:2 molar ratio in B16F10 cells (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative western blotting data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The concentration of CP in B16F10 cells is ~1 µM.
source: Previous studies reported the concentration of CP in B16F10 cells to be ~1 µM (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Pollard and Borisy, 2003), suggesting that mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2014 and Pollard and Borisy, 2003.

claim: mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM in B16F10 cells.
source: Previous studies reported the concentration of CP in B16F10 cells to be ~1 µM (Fujiwara et al., 2014; Pollard and Borisy, 2003), suggesting that mTwf1 is present at ~0.5 µM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 1:2 molar ratio of Twinfilin to CP (Figure 6C) and the reported CP concentration of ~1 µM.

claim: The Twinfilin-CP interaction has a Kd of 50 nM.
source: Given the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd = 50 nM), these observations are consistent with mTwf1 being associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
evidence: This is based on binding data from the manuscript (Figure 1B).

claim: mTwf1 is associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
source: Given the high affinity of the Twinfilin-CP interaction (Kd = 50 nM), these observations are consistent with mTwf1 being associated with a substantial fraction of the CP in cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high affinity of the interaction (Kd = 50 nM) and the cellular concentrations of both proteins.

claim: Knockdown of either mTwf1 or CP led to a marked increase in the density of peripheral protrusions or microspikes with a concomitant loss of lamellipodial surfaces.
source: Knockdown of either mTwf1 or CP led to a similar, marked increase in the density of peripheral protrusions or microspikes with a concomitant loss of lamellipodial surfaces (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Similar phenotypes have been reported for CP depletion in multiple cell lines.
source: Similar phenotypes have been reported for CP depletion in multiple cell lines (Edwards et al., 2013; Edwards et al., 2015; Mejillano et al., 2004; Sinnar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Edwards et al., 2013; Edwards et al., 2015; Mejillano et al., 2004; Sinnar et al., 2014.

claim: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1.
source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Expression of mTwf1-11 did not rescue the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1.
source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: The cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
source: Expression of an RNAi-refractive mTwf1 construct, but not mTwf1-11, rescued the defects caused by depletion of endogenous mTwf1 (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that these cellular functions of mTwf1 critically depend on its interaction with CP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that wild-type mTwf1 but not mTwf1-11 (which doesn't bind CP) rescues the knockdown phenotype.

claim: Knockdown of CP was accompanied by a dramatic reduction in Twinfilin levels in cells.
source: We also made the unexpected observation that knockdown of CP was accompanied by a dramatic reduction in Twinfilin levels in cells, as seen by both western blotting (Figure 6D) and immunofluorescence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6D and immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction in Twinfilin levels upon CP knockdown was confirmed using a second RNAi oligonucleotide that targets a different region of CP.
source: This effect was confirmed using a second RNAi oligonucleotide that targets a different region of CP (siCP2, Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The reduction in Twinfilin levels upon CP knockdown was observed in additional cell lines besides B16F10, including Neuro-2A and NIH-3T3 cells.
source: Further, it was observed in additional cell lines besides B16F10, including Neuro-2A and NIH-3T3 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blotting data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion.
source: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion, indicating that a portion of the original defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments described in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A portion of the defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
source: Forced expression of mTwf1 partially rescued the defects associated with CP depletion, indicating that a portion of the original defects observed after CP knockdown were likely due to the accompanying loss of mTwf1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the partial rescue of CP knockdown phenotype by mTwf1 overexpression.

claim: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP.
source: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP, and ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects caused by CARMIL1 overexpression.
source: B16F10 cells ectopically expressing CARMIL1 showed morphological defects similar to loss of CP, and ectopic mTwf1 expression rescued the defects (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Ectopic expression of mTwf1 alone caused no significant change in cell morphology.
source: Importantly, ectopic expression of mTwf1 alone caused no significant change in cell morphology.
evidence: This is based on the cell morphology data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: Twf1 promotes capping in vivo, at least in part by competing with CARMIL for CP binding and antagonizing the uncapping effects of CARMIL.
source: These results support our biochemical observations, and suggest that Twf1 promotes capping in vivo, at least in part by competing with CARMIL for CP binding and antagonizing the uncapping effects of CARMIL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue of CARMIL1 overexpression phenotype by mTwf1 (Figure 7A-B).

claim: Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the collective data showing Twinfilin has a CPI-like motif and competes with CARMIL.

claim: Twinfilin is the first CPI-motif protein to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Twinfilin binding doesn't weaken CP capping activity (Figure 1) unlike other CPI proteins.

claim: Twinfilin is the first CPI-motif protein to antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that Twinfilin is a new member of the CPI-motif family of proteins, and the first within this group to show the ability to bind CP without reducing CP affinity for barbed ends, and antagonize the negative regulatory effects of another CPI protein.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing Twinfilin protects CP from CARMIL (Figure 3).

claim: The Fujiwara model posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state.
source: The best working model to date has been the Fujiwara model (Fujiwara et al., 2014) (depicted here as 'Earlier Model'; Figure 7C). It posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state, which then can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.
evidence: This is a description of the Fujiwara model based on citation to Fujiwara et al., 2014.

claim: In the Fujiwara model, CP can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.
source: The best working model to date has been the Fujiwara model (Fujiwara et al., 2014) (depicted here as 'Earlier Model'; Figure 7C). It posits that the majority of CP in the cytosol is bound to V-1, in an inactive state, which then can be locally 'activated' by CARMIL at the leading edge.
evidence: This is a description of the Fujiwara model based on citation to Fujiwara et al., 2014.

claim: CP-CARMIL complexes have ~100 fold reduced affinity for barbed ends compared to free CP.
source: However, a caveat to this model is that it suggests CP-CARMIL complexes are the dominant capping species in the cell, despite this complex having ~100 fold reduced affinity for barbed ends compared to free CP.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about CARMIL's effect on CP affinity for barbed ends.

claim: Twinfilin's protective effects on CP allow cells to maintain a larger pool of fully active CP (Twinfilin-CP complexes) in the cytosol than was previously thought.
source: In light of our results, we propose several additions and revisions to the Fujiwara model (see 'Revised Model'; Figure 7D). First, we suggest that Twinfilin's protective effects on CP, in particular against V-1, allow cells to maintain a larger pool of fully active CP (Twinfilin-CP complexes) in the cytosol than was previously thought.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective data from the manuscript.

claim: V-1 functions to maintain a cytosolic reservoir of inactive CP, mobilized by Twinfilin and/or CARMIL dissociating V-1.
source: Second, we propose that V-1 functions to maintain a cytosolic reservoir of inactive CP, mobilized by Twinfilin and/or CARMIL dissociating V-1 to generate 'stable capping' (Twinfilin-CP) in the cytosol and possibly 'transient capping' (CARMIL-CP) complexes at the plasma membrane, respectively.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the collective data from the manuscript.

claim: CARMIL-CP complexes at the plasma membrane could facilitate actin network growth to drive leading edge protrusion.
source: CARMIL-CP complexes at the plasma membrane could facilitate actin network growth to drive leading edge protrusion.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the known localization and function of CARMIL.

claim: Twinfilin-CP complexes in the cytosol may facilitate stable capping of barbed ends to limit network growth and promote filament disassembly and turnover.
source: In contrast, Twinfilin-CP complexes in the cytosol may facilitate stable capping of barbed ends to limit network growth and promote filament disassembly and turnover.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the data showing Twinfilin protects CP from inhibitors.

claim: The association of Twinfilin-CP complexes with barbed ends primes filaments for disassembly.
source: Third, we propose that the association of Twinfilin-CP complexes with barbed ends primes filaments for disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the known depolymerization activity of Twinfilin.

claim: CARMIL and/or other CPI proteins may competitively remove CP from barbed ends, leaving Twinfilin at the barbed end to processively depolymerize filaments.
source: Our data show that CARMIL, and/or other CPI proteins, compete with Twinfilin for binding CP. These interactions may competitively remove CP from barbed ends, leaving Twinfilin at the barbed end to processively depolymerize filaments, either alone or in combination with Srv2/CAP (as depicted in Figure 6D) (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the competition data and known activities of Twinfilin.

claim: The interaction of Twinfilin with CP could serve to initially promote capping and also to position Twinfilin at barbed ends for subsequently catalyzing the disassembly of filaments.
source: In this manner, the interaction of Twinfilin with CP could serve not only to initially promote capping, and thus limit network growth, but also to position Twinfilin at barbed ends for subsequently catalyzing the disassembly of filaments.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal integrating the pro-capping and depolymerization functions of Twinfilin.

claim: Functions of mammalian Twinfilin and CP are closely intertwined.
source: In summary, our results show that functions of mammalian Twinfilin and CP are closely intertwined.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the collective data from the manuscript.

claim: The functional relationship between Twinfilin and CP is likely to extend to other species given CPI motif sequence conservation in the Twinfilin tail region and the conserved nature of the Twinfilin-CP interaction.
source: This functional relationship is likely to extend to other species given CPI motif sequence conservation in the Twinfilin tail region (Figure 2A) and the conserved nature of the Twinfilin-CP interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on sequence conservation data (Figure 2A) and known conservation of the Twinfilin-CP interaction.

claim: S. cerevisiae Aim21 was recently identified as the first yeast CPI motif-containing protein.
source: Indeed, S. cerevisiae Aim21 was recently identified as the first yeast CPI motif-containing protein, and was shown to regulate CP function at cortical actin patches (Farrell et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Farrell et al., 2017 and Shin et al., 2018.

claim: Aim21 was shown to regulate CP function at cortical actin patches.
source: Indeed, S. cerevisiae Aim21 was recently identified as the first yeast CPI motif-containing protein, and was shown to regulate CP function at cortical actin patches (Farrell et al., 2017; Shin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Farrell et al., 2017 and Shin et al., 2018.

claim: In the structural model, the Twinfilin tail is long enough to allow for simultaneous binding of Twinfilin's CPI motif to CP and Twinfilin's C-terminal ADFH domain to an actin subunit at the barbed end.
source: In this model, the Twinfilin tail is long enough to allow for simultaneous binding of Twinfilin's CPI motif to CP and Twinfilin's C-terminal ADFH domain to an actin subunit at the barbed end.
evidence: This is based on the structural model shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no clashes in binding between CP and Twinfilin on actin in the structural model.
source: Further, there are no clashes in binding between CP and Twinfilin on actin.
evidence: This is based on the structural model shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: CP and Twinfilin appear to be able to associate with barbed ends individually or as a CP-Twinfilin complex, but with distinct consequences for the function and dynamics of actin networks.
source: It is worth noting that CP and Twinfilin appear to be able to associate with barbed ends individually or as a CP-Twinfilin complex, but with distinct consequences for the function and dynamics of actin networks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data from the manuscript.

claim: CP alone stably caps barbed ends, blocking subunit addition or loss.
source: CP alone stably caps barbed ends, blocking subunit addition or loss, and our results suggest that CP-Twinfilin complexes may do the same.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CP function.

claim: CP-Twinfilin complexes may stably cap barbed ends, blocking subunit addition or loss.
source: CP alone stably caps barbed ends, blocking subunit addition or loss, and our results suggest that CP-Twinfilin complexes may do the same.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the data showing Twinfilin protects CP from inhibitors.

claim: When Twinfilin alone associates with barbed ends, it drives processive depolymerization, while blocking new assembly.
source: However, when Twinfilin alone associates with barbed ends, it drives processive depolymerization, while blocking new assembly (Hilton et al., 2018; Johnston et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hilton et al., 2018 and Johnston et al., 2015.

claim: Despite key differences in the nature of their associations with barbed ends, CP and Twinfilin each inhibit filament growth.
source: Thus, despite key differences in the nature of their associations with barbed ends, CP and Twinfilin each inhibit filament growth, likely explaining why Twinfilin can replace CP in reconstituted actin motility assays in vitro (Helfer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known activities of CP and Twinfilin.

claim: Twinfilin can replace CP in reconstituted actin motility assays in vitro.
source: Thus, despite key differences in the nature of their associations with barbed ends, CP and Twinfilin each inhibit filament growth, likely explaining why Twinfilin can replace CP in reconstituted actin motility assays in vitro (Helfer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Helfer et al., 2006.

claim: Actin dynamics in vivo are controlled by a complex set of barbed end-associated factors, many of which interact with each other and/or stimulate each other's dissociation from barbed ends.
source: Finally, our data add to a broader emerging view that actin dynamics in vivo are controlled by a complex set of barbed end-associated factors, many of which interact with each other and/or stimulate each other's dissociation from barbed ends.
evidence: This is a broader interpretive statement based on the data from this manuscript and the broader literature.

claim: Multi-component mechanisms may allow cells to control rapid transitions at filament ends through different functional states.
source: These multi-component mechanisms may allow cells to control rapid transitions at filament ends through different functional states, including (i) formin-bound elongation, (ii) paused growth by formin-CP 'decision complexes', (iii) stable or transiently capped states by CP alone or CP-Twinfilin complexes (Bombardier et al., 2015; Shekhar et al., 2015), and (iv) depolymerization by Twinfilin, Cofilin, and/or Srv2/CAP.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal integrating the findings of this study with broader knowledge of actin regulation.

claim: Molecular mechanisms for regulating barbed end growth are vastly more elaborate and dynamic than once thought.
source: These molecular mechanisms for regulating barbed end growth are vastly more elaborate and dynamic than once thought, and help explain the exquisite spatiotemporal control that cells have in tuning actin network dynamics.
evidence: This is a summary statement reflecting on the implications of the findings.
